name: Diethylpropion

lead: Diethylpropion (amfepramone) is an older prescription appetite suppressant that reduces hunger so people eat less and lose weight, working toward a leaner look.

The body converts it to ethcathinone, which mainly affects norepinephrine signalling. In the US it is labelled as a short-term add-on, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted diet for people with a BMI of 30 or higher. Meta-analyses of weight-loss drugs have included it alongside phentermine and sibutramine.

paras: It is taken as a pill under prescription for a few weeks alongside dieting. It is discussed with other older diet drugs.

The label lists raised heart rate and blood pressure, arrhythmia and rare pulmonary hypertension, with a cited association for anorectic use beyond three months. It is Schedule IV in the US, and in June 2022 the EMA's safety committee recommended withdrawing it from the EU market.

angle.text: Diethylpropion is a stimulant appetite suppressant that lowers calorie intake and leads to weight loss and a leaner look. It is an older prescription medication labelled for a few weeks of use.

lead: Diethylpropion, also called amfepramone, is a prescription appetite suppressant of the phenethylamine and cathinone families. The US label indicates it as a short-term adjunct, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted regimen for people with a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet or exercise alone. [1][2]

It is a prodrug of ethcathinone and is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US. [2] In June 2022 the European Medicines Agency's safety committee recommended withdrawing marketing authorisations for amfepramone medicines, according to Wikipedia. [2]
Meta-analyses of weight-loss drugs have included diethylpropion alongside phentermine and sibutramine. [3] No community material about it is catalogued here.
infobox: Tenuate, Tepanil, Nobesine, Regenon and others [2]

paras: The label for extended-release diethylpropion describes management of exogenous obesity as a short-term adjunct (a few weeks) in patients with BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet or exercise alone. [1] The 2022 American Gastroenterological Association guideline on pharmacological interventions for obesity forms part of the current clinical context for such drugs. [4]

The label lists precordial pain, arrhythmia, ECG changes, tachycardia, raised blood pressure and palpitation, with rare reports of pulmonary hypertension. [1] It warns against combination with other anorectics and cites a case-control study associating anorectic use beyond three months with a 23-fold increase in pulmonary hypertension risk. [1] Valvulopathy has been very rarely reported with diethylpropion monotherapy, with causality uncertain. [1] Reviews of anti-obesity drug safety discuss the class's cardiovascular and abuse-related concerns. [5][6]

Wikipedia states diethylpropion has no meaningful affinity for monoamine transporters itself and acts through ethcathinone, which affects norepinephrine roughly ten times more than dopamine and twenty times more than serotonin. [2] Elimination half-life of metabolites is given as about 4 to 6 hours. [2] Early animal research examined self-administration of stimulants including this class. [7]

Legal status varies: Schedule IV in the US, Class C in the UK, prescription-only in Germany and Australia, and Schedule IV in Canada. [2] Studies cited on Wikipedia describe its abuse potential as relatively low. [2]

A 2005 meta-analysis of pharmacologic obesity treatments included pooled analyses of diethylpropion together with sibutramine and phentermine. [3] A registered phase 4 trial, the Louisiana Obese Subjects Study, examined non-surgical weight loss in severe obesity but was terminated. [8] No studies found of diethylpropion specifically for appearance-related goals.

timeline.event: EMA safety committee recommended withdrawing amfepramone authorisations, per Wikipedia. [2]
